notes.meaning: Joseph threw himself onto his father's body and wept, giving Jacob a final kiss of deep love and sorrow. It was the duty and privilege of the chief son to close his father's eyes and say goodbye. True faith does not take away our sorrow when loved ones die, but lets us grieve with love and respect.

Joseph ordered his personal physicians to embalm Jacob's body. Embalming involved using special oils and spices to preserve the body so it would not decay. This was standard practice in Egypt, but it was also necessary because Jacob needed to be carried on a long journey to Canaan for burial.

The embalming process took forty full days to complete properly. The Egyptians joined in mourning Jacob for seventy days, which was nearly the time given to mourn an Egyptian king. This extended period of public grief showed how deeply Pharaoh and his people respected Joseph and his father.

After the seventy days of mourning ended, Joseph asked members of Pharaoh's court to carry a message to the king. A person wearing mourning clothes and with uncut hair was not permitted to enter the king's royal presence. Joseph explained that Jacob had bound him by a solemn oath to bury him in Canaan, and he promised Pharaoh that he would return as soon as the funeral was done.

Pharaoh readily granted Joseph permission to make the long trip to Canaan. Even among rulers of other nations, a sacred oath made to a dying father was treated with the highest respect. Pharaoh trusted Joseph completely and released his top official to honor his promise.

An immense state funeral procession left Egypt to accompany Jacob's body to Canaan. Royal officials, court elders, chariots, and horsemen traveled alongside Jacob's sons to show honor and provide protection through the desert. The families left their small children and livestock in Goshen, making it clear to everyone that they planned to return.

The massive group stopped at the threshing floor of Atad near the border of Canaan to hold an intense week of loud lamentation. The local Canaanites watched the solemn ceremony and assumed it was an Egyptian national mourning because of all the royal officials present. Because of this, they named the site Abel-mizraim, which means 'the mourning of Egypt.'

Jacob's sons carried out their father's dying wish by taking his body all the way to Machpelah. They laid him to rest in the family cave beside Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, and Leah. This was the only piece of the Promised Land that Abraham had legally purchased, standing as a quiet sign of their faith in God's future promises.

After the burial was finished, Joseph and his brothers kept their word and returned to Egypt together with the entire escort. Although Canaan was the land God had promised them, the appointed time for Israel to possess it had not yet arrived. They went back to Goshen to wait for God's timing.

With Jacob gone, the brothers were suddenly gripped by fear and guilt over what they had done decades earlier. They worried that Joseph had only treated them kindly out of respect for their father. A guilty conscience often makes people expect the worst, assuming that others will seek revenge the moment they have the chance.

The brothers sent a message begging Joseph for forgiveness, appealing to Jacob's memory and their shared faith in God. They openly acknowledged their sin without making excuses, though they may have invented their father's quote out of sheer desperation. Joseph wept when he heard it, deeply pained that his brothers still doubted his love and feared his anger.

The brothers came in person and threw themselves on the floor before Joseph, offering to become his slaves. In doing so, they fulfilled the dreams Joseph had dreamed as a boy, when he saw their sheaves and stars bowing to him. They offered to give up their freedom to make up for having sold him into slavery so long ago.

Joseph immediately calmed their fears and told them not to be afraid of him. He asked if he was in God's place, recognizing that judging wrongdoers and taking vengeance belongs to God alone. Joseph refused to hold power over them as their punisher, leaving justice in the Lord's hands.

differ.view: God sovereignly planned and ordained the event itself for good, while the human actors remained fully responsible for their evil motives.
God did not cause or plan the sin, but in His wisdom He permitted it and redirected its results toward a good end.

notes.meaning: Joseph did not pretend his brothers were innocent, for their original plans had truly been wicked. Yet God had worked above their cruel actions, directing the whole story to bring about salvation and save many people from starvation. God's good purpose was far greater and stronger than their evil schemes.

differ.view: God did not merely react to human sin, but sovereignly planned the very events for a good purpose.
God overruled the wicked choices of the brothers to turn their evil into a blessing for the family.

notes.meaning: Joseph backed up his forgiveness with practical care, promising to feed and protect his brothers and their families. He spoke gently and tenderly to their hearts so they would feel entirely secure. True forgiveness does not hold people on probation, but comforts them and treats them with genuine kindness.

Joseph lived in Egypt to the ripe age of 110, which was regarded in Egyptian culture as the ideal full life. God blessed him to see his great-grandchildren through Ephraim and his great-grandchildren through Manasseh. Placing these newborn babies on his knees was a loving custom that showed he welcomed and claimed them as his own family.

As his death drew near, Joseph gathered his family to remind them of God's unshakable covenant. Even though he had spent most of his life in Egypt, he knew Egypt was never meant to be their permanent home. He assured them that God would step in and lead them back to the land He had sworn to give their ancestors.

Joseph made the Israelites promise under oath that when God brought them out of Egypt, they would take his bones with them. He did not ask to be buried in Canaan right away like Jacob was, but wanted his remains to wait for the national return. This command was a bold act of faith showing he was certain God's promises would come true.

Joseph died peacefully at 110 years old, bringing the generation of the patriarchs to an end. His body was embalmed and placed in an Egyptian wooden coffin, where it stayed above ground as a constant reminder of the Promised Land. The book of Genesis closes with a coffin in Egypt, pointing ahead to the rescue that God would bring in Exodus.
